p.src: Now Xu Huang led his army across the Han River. Ignoring Wang Ping's earnest remonstrance, he crossed the river and made camp. Huang Zhong and Zhao Yun said to Xuande, “Each of us will lead his own troops out to meet Cao Cao's army.” Xuande consented. The two men led their troops away. Huang Zhong said to Zhao Yun, “Xu Huang has come relying on his valor, so let us refrain from engaging him for now; when dusk falls and his men are weary, you and I can divide our forces and strike from two directions.” Zhao Yun agreed, and each took command of a force and held fast behind the camp stockades. Xu Huang brought his troops forward to challenge them from the hour of the dragon until the hour of the monkey, yet the Shu army made no move. Xu Huang then ordered all his crossbowmen forward to shoot into the Shu camp. Huang Zhong said to Zhao Yun, “Xu Huang has ordered his bowmen to shoot; his army must be preparing to withdraw. We should seize this moment to strike.” Before he had finished speaking, a report suddenly came that the rear ranks of Cao Cao's army were indeed beginning to retreat. At once the drums thundered through the Shu camp: Huang Zhong led his troops out on the left, and Zhao Yun led his out on the right. Attacked from both sides, Xu Huang suffered a crushing defeat. His soldiers were driven into the Han River, and countless men perished. Xu Huang fought desperately and escaped. Returning to camp, he rebuked Wang Ping: “When you saw my army in grave danger, why did you not come to its aid?” Wang Ping replied, “Had I gone to your aid, this camp could not have been held either. I advised you not to go, but you refused to listen, and so brought about this defeat.” Xu Huang flew into a rage and intended to kill Wang Ping. That night Wang Ping led his own troops in setting fire to the camp. Cao Cao's soldiers fell into chaos, and Xu Huang abandoned the camp and fled. Wang Ping crossed the Han River and surrendered to Zhao Yun, who brought him before Xuande. Wang Ping explained the whole geography of the Han River region. Xuande was delighted and said, “With Wang Zijun in my service, there can be no doubt that I shall take Hanzhong.” He appointed Wang Ping General of the Household and placed him in command of the guides.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xu Huang fled back to Cao Cao and reported that Wang Ping had defected and surrendered to Liu Bei. Cao Cao was furious and personally led his great army to seize the stockaded camp by the Han River. Fearing that his isolated force could not hold its ground, Zhao Yun withdrew west of the Han River. The two armies faced each other across the river. Xuande and Kongming came to survey the situation. Upstream on the Han River, Kongming saw a line of earthen hills capable of concealing more than a thousand men. Returning to camp, he summoned Zhao Yun and instructed him: “Take five hundred men, all equipped with drums and horns, and conceal them below those earthen hills. Whether at midnight or at dusk, whenever you hear a cannon signal from my camp, beat the drums once for each report—but on no account come out to fight.” Zilong accepted the plan and departed. Kongming secretly watched from atop a high hill.

p.src: The next day Cao Cao's soldiers came to challenge them, but not a single man emerged from the Shu camp, nor did its archers loose a single bolt. Cao Cao's troops returned to their camp. Late that night, when Kongming saw the lights in Cao Cao's camp go out and the soldiers settle to rest, he gave the signal. When Zilong heard it, he ordered the drums and horns sounded together. Cao Cao's soldiers panicked, certain that their camp was being raided. But when they came out of camp, not an enemy unit was to be seen. Just as they returned to camp and were about to rest, the signal sounded again, the drums and horns blared once more, and battle cries shook the earth and echoed through the valleys. Cao Cao's army had no peace all night. After three successive nights of such alarms and uncertainty, Cao Cao lost his nerve, struck camp, withdrew thirty li, and encamped on open ground. Kongming laughed and said, “Though Cao Cao understands the art of war, he does not understand deceptive stratagems.” He then asked Xuande to cross the Han River in person and establish a camp with the river at his back. Xuande asked what his plan was, and Kongming explained it to him in detail.

p.src: When Cao Cao saw Xuande encamp with the river at his back, he grew suspicious and sent a man with a written challenge. Kongming wrote his reply, accepting battle on the following day. The next day the two armies met before Wujie Mountain on the road between their camps and drew up their battle lines. Cao Cao rode out and halted beneath his command banner. Dragon and phoenix standards stood arrayed in two lines; after three rolls of the drums, he called for Xuande to parley. Xuande came forward accompanied by Liu Feng, Meng Da, and the other generals of Sichuan. Cao Cao brandished his whip and cursed him: “Liu Bei, you ungrateful, faithless traitor who has rebelled against the court!” Xuande replied, “I am a kinsman of the imperial house of Han, and I wage war against traitors by imperial command. You murdered the Empress Dowager and made yourself a king, usurping the imperial carriage of the Son of Heaven. If that is not rebellion, what is?” Enraged, Cao Cao ordered Xu Huang to ride out and fight. Liu Feng rode out to meet him. As they fought, Xuande was the first to withdraw into his formation. Unable to withstand Xu Huang, Liu Feng wheeled his horse and fled. Cao Cao gave the order: “Whoever captures Liu Bei shall be made King of Western Sichuan.” With a mighty shout, the whole army charged through the enemy lines. The Shu soldiers fled toward the Han River, abandoning all their camps; horses and weapons lay strewn all along the road. Cao Cao's soldiers all scrambled to seize them. Cao Cao hastily sounded the gong to recall his army. His generals said, “We were just about to capture Liu Bei. Why has Your Majesty recalled us?” Cao Cao replied, “That the Shu army camped with the Han River at its back is the first cause for suspicion; that they abandoned so many horses and weapons is the second. Withdraw at once, and touch none of the goods.” He then issued an order: “Anyone who takes so much as a single object without leave shall be beheaded at once. Retreat with all speed.” Just as Cao Cao's soldiers turned back, Kongming's signal banner rose. Xuande led the central army forth, Huang Zhong attacked from the left, and Zhao Yun from the right. Cao Cao's army broke and fled, and Kongming pursued them throughout the night.

p.src: Cao Cao ordered the army to fall back to Nanzheng. Suddenly fires arose along five routes. It turned out that Wei Yan and Zhang Fei had left Yan Yan to guard Langzhong in their stead, divided their troops, and attacked, taking Nanzheng before Cao Cao arrived. Cao Cao was alarmed and fled toward Yangping Pass. Xuande's great army pursued as far as Nanzheng and Baozhou. After order had been restored among the people, Xuande asked Kongming, “Why was Cao Cao defeated so swiftly on this campaign?” Kongming replied, “Cao Cao has always been suspicious by nature. Though skilled in war, his suspicions often lead him to defeat. I defeated him with feigned forces designed to arouse doubt.” Xuande said, “Now Cao Cao has withdrawn to defend Yangping Pass, his position is isolated. What strategy will you use to drive him away, Master?” Kongming replied, “I have already calculated everything.” He sent Zhang Fei and Wei Yan by separate routes to cut Cao Cao's supply lines, and ordered Huang Zhong and Zhao Yun to divide their forces and set fire to the mountains along two other routes. The generals of the four forces departed, each leading local guides and troops.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Cao withdrew to defend Yangping Pass and sent scouts to reconnoiter. They returned and reported, “The Shu army has blocked every path, near and far; every place where we might gather firewood has been utterly burned; yet we do not know where their troops are.” While Cao Cao was still perplexed, another report came that Zhang Fei and Wei Yan had divided their forces and were raiding the supply convoys. Cao Cao asked, “Who dares face Zhang Fei?” Xu Chu said, “I am willing to go!” Cao Cao ordered Xu Chu to lead a thousand picked troops along the road from Yangping Pass to escort the provisions through. When the officer in charge of the convoy met him, he said with delight, “Had you not come, General, these provisions could never have reached Yangping.” He then presented Xu Chu with the wine and meat carried on the wagons. Xu Chu drank deeply and soon became very drunk. In high spirits from the wine, he urged the provision wagons onward. The convoy officer said, “The sun has already set. The mountains ahead around Baozhou are steep and perilous; we should not attempt to pass through yet.” Xu Chu replied, “I possess the valor to face ten thousand men. Why should I fear anyone? Tonight the moonlight is perfect for moving the provision wagons.” Xu Chu rode at the head, saber held crosswise, and led the troops forward. After the second watch, they proceeded along the road toward Baozhou. Halfway there, drums and horns suddenly thundered from a hollow in the mountains, and a force barred their path. The general at their head was none other than Zhang Fei; leveling his spear and spurring his horse, he charged straight at Xu Chu. Xu Chu brandished his saber and met the attack, but in his drunken state he could not withstand Zhang Fei. After only a few exchanges, Zhang Fei struck him in the shoulder with his spear, and he tumbled from his horse. His soldiers hurriedly rescued him, then turned and fled. Zhang Fei seized all the provisions and wagons and returned.

p.src: Meanwhile, the generals escorted Xu Chu back to Cao Cao. Cao Cao ordered the physicians to tend his wound, while he personally led his troops out to seek a decisive battle with the Shu army. Xuande led his army out to meet him. When the two armies had drawn up opposite each other, Xuande ordered Liu Feng to ride forth. Cao Cao reviled him: “You sandal-peddling brat, forever sending your adopted son to face the enemy! If I summon my Yellow-bearded Boy, he will pound your adopted son into pulp!” Liu Feng flew into a rage, leveled his spear, spurred his horse, and charged straight at Cao Cao. Cao Cao ordered Xu Huang to meet him, whereupon Liu Feng feigned defeat and fled. Cao Cao led his men in pursuit, but from the Shu camp cannon signals suddenly sounded on every side, while drums and horns blared together. Fearing an ambush, Cao Cao hastily ordered a retreat. Cao Cao’s soldiers trampled one another, and a great many died. They fled back to Yangping Pass and had barely settled down when the Shu army reached the walls, setting fires at the east gate and raising battle cries at the west; at the south gate they set more fires, and at the north they beat the drums. Cao Cao was greatly alarmed and abandoned the pass in flight. The Shu troops pursued and attacked from behind. As Cao Cao fled, Zhang Fei appeared ahead with one force to bar his way, Zhao Yun attacked from the rear with another, and Huang Zhong brought yet another army against him from Baozhou. Cao Cao suffered a crushing defeat. His generals guarded him as they fought their way out and fled. They had just escaped to the mouth of Xie Valley when a cloud of dust suddenly rose ahead and a body of troops approached. Cao Cao said, “If these are ambush troops, I am finished!” When the troops drew near, however, they proved to be led by Cao Cao’s second son, Cao Zhang.

p.src: Cao Zhang’s courtesy name was Ziwen, and from youth he had excelled at riding and archery; his physical strength surpassed that of ordinary men, and he could grapple fierce beasts with his bare hands. Cao Cao once admonished him: “You neglect books and delight only in bows and horses. That is merely the valor of a common fighting man—what is there to prize in it?” Cao Zhang replied, “A true man should emulate Wei Qing and Huo Qubing, win glory in the desert, and lead hundreds of thousands on sweeping campaigns across the realm; how could I become a mere scholar?” Cao Cao once asked his sons about their ambitions. Cao Zhang said, “I wish to be a general.” Cao Cao asked, “What manner of general?” Cao Zhang replied, “Clad in stout armor and bearing keen weapons, I would face peril without thought for myself and lead the soldiers from the front; rewards would unfailingly be granted and punishments unfailingly enforced.” Cao Cao laughed heartily. In the twenty-third year of Jian’an, the Wuhuan of Dai Commandery rebelled, and Cao Cao ordered Cao Zhang to lead fifty thousand troops against them; before his departure, Cao Cao warned him: “‘At home we are father and son; when entrusted with an office, we are sovereign and subject.’ The law shows no partiality to affection. Take this deeply to heart.” Cao Zhang reached the region north of Dai, led the charge in person, and fought all the way to Sanggan, pacifying the entire north; then, hearing that Cao Cao had been defeated at Yangping, he came to assist him in battle. Cao Cao was overjoyed to see him and said, “Now that my Yellow-bearded Boy has come, Liu Bei will surely be defeated!” He therefore rallied his troops, turned back, and encamped at the mouth of Xie Valley. A messenger reported to Xuande that Cao Zhang had arrived. Xuande asked, “Who dares go and fight Cao Zhang?” Liu Feng said, “I am willing to go.” Meng Da also asked to go. Xuande said, “Go together, the two of you, and let us see who wins the merit.” Each led five thousand troops to meet the enemy, Liu Feng in front and Meng Da behind. Cao Zhang rode out and engaged Liu Feng; after only three bouts, Liu Feng was soundly defeated and withdrew. Meng Da led his troops forward and was just about to engage when he saw Cao Cao’s army fall into great disorder. It turned out that the armies of Ma Chao and Wu Lan had attacked, throwing Cao Cao’s troops into panic. Meng Da led his troops in a converging attack. Ma Chao’s soldiers had long husbanded their strength; now they displayed their might and valor with irresistible force. Cao Cao’s troops were defeated and fled. Cao Zhang encountered Wu Lan, and after the two had fought only a few bouts, Cao Zhang thrust his halberd and struck Wu Lan from his horse. All three armies became embroiled in a melee. Cao Cao gathered his forces and established a firm camp at the mouth of Xie Valley.

p.src: Cao Cao remained encamped for many days. He wished to advance, but Ma Chao barred his way; he wished to withdraw, but feared the ridicule of the Shu army, and so remained irresolute. Just then, the cook brought in chicken soup. Seeing a chicken rib in the bowl, Cao Cao was moved to reflection. While he was pondering, Xiahou Dun entered the tent and requested the password for the night. Cao Cao casually replied, “Chicken rib! Chicken rib!” Xiahou Dun passed the order to all the officers, and they all used “Chicken rib” as the password. When Yang Xiu, registrar of the marching army, heard that the words “Chicken rib” had been issued, he ordered the accompanying soldiers to pack their baggage and prepare for the journey home. Someone reported this to Xiahou Dun. Greatly startled, Xiahou Dun summoned Yang Xiu to his tent and asked, “Why are you packing your baggage?” Yang Xiu replied, “From tonight’s password, it is plain that the King of Wei will withdraw and return before many days have passed. A chicken rib has no meat worth eating, yet still has some savor when cast aside. At present we cannot prevail by advancing, yet fear ridicule if we retreat; remaining here is useless, so it would be better to return early. Tomorrow the King of Wei will surely order the army home. Therefore I packed in advance, to avoid confusion when the time comes to depart.” Xiahou Dun said, “You truly understand the King of Wei’s innermost thoughts!” He too began packing his baggage. Thereupon every general in the camp began preparing to return. That night, Cao Cao’s mind was in turmoil and he could not sleep soundly, so he took up his steel axe and walked secretly around the camp. He saw the soldiers in Xiahou Dun’s camp all packing their baggage. Cao Cao was greatly startled, hurried back to his tent, summoned Xiahou Dun, and asked the reason. Xiahou Dun replied, “The registrar, Yang Dezu, discerned in advance Your Majesty’s intention to return.” Cao Cao summoned Yang Xiu and questioned him, and Yang Xiu explained the meaning of “chicken rib.” Cao Cao flew into a rage and cried, “How dare you fabricate words and unsettle the morale of my army!” He shouted for the executioners to drag Yang Xiu out and behead him, then had his head displayed outside the camp gate as a warning.

he wished to withdraw, but feared the ridicule of the Shu army, and so remained irresolute.
Just then, the cook brought in chicken soup.
Seeing a chicken rib in the bowl, Cao Cao was moved to reflection.
While he was pondering, Xiahou Dun entered the tent and requested the password for the night.
Cao Cao casually replied, “Chicken rib!
Chicken rib!”
Xiahou Dun passed the order to all the officers, and they all used “Chicken rib” as the password.
When Yang Xiu, registrar of the marching army, heard that the words “Chicken rib” had been issued, he ordered the accompanying soldiers to pack their baggage and prepare for the journey home.
Someone reported this to Xiahou Dun.
Greatly startled, Xiahou Dun summoned Yang Xiu to his tent and asked, “Why are you packing your baggage?”

Yang Xiu replied, “From tonight’s password, it is plain that the King of Wei will withdraw and return before many days have passed. A chicken rib has no meat worth eating, yet still has some savor when cast aside.
At present we cannot prevail by advancing, yet fear ridicule if we retreat; remaining here is useless, so it would be better to return early.
Tomorrow the King of Wei will surely order the army home.
Therefore I packed in advance, to avoid confusion when the time comes to depart.”
Xiahou Dun said, “You truly understand the King of Wei’s innermost thoughts!”
He too began packing his baggage.
Thereupon every general in the camp began preparing to return.
That night, Cao Cao’s mind was in turmoil and he could not sleep soundly, so he took up his steel axe and walked secretly around the camp.
He saw the soldiers in Xiahou Dun’s camp all packing their baggage.
Cao Cao was greatly startled, hurried back to his tent, summoned Xiahou Dun, and asked the reason.
Xiahou Dun replied, “The registrar, Yang Dezu, discerned in advance Your Majesty’s intention to return.”
Cao Cao summoned Yang Xiu and questioned him, and Yang Xiu explained the meaning of “chicken rib.”
Cao Cao flew into a rage and cried, “How dare you fabricate words and unsettle the morale of my army!”
He shouted for the executioners to drag Yang Xiu out and behead him, then had his head displayed outside the camp gate as a warning.

p.src: In truth, Yang Xiu was proud of his talents and unrestrained in conduct, and had repeatedly aroused Cao Cao’s jealousy. Cao Cao once had a garden built; when it was finished, he went to inspect it, but offered neither praise nor blame. He merely took a brush, wrote the character “活” on the gate, and departed. No one understood what he meant. Yang Xiu said, “Add the character ‘活’ inside ‘門,’ and it forms the character ‘闊,’ meaning ‘wide.’ The Chancellor merely finds the garden gate too wide.” Thereupon the surrounding wall and gate were rebuilt. When the alterations were complete, Cao Cao was invited to inspect them again. Cao Cao was delighted and asked, “Who understood my meaning?” His attendants replied, “Yang Xiu.” Though Cao Cao praised him, inwardly he became deeply jealous. On another day, a box of butter cakes arrived from beyond the northern frontier. Cao Cao himself wrote the three characters “一合酥” on the box and placed it on his desk. Yang Xiu came in, saw it, and at once took a spoon and divided the contents among everyone, who ate it all. When Cao Cao asked why, Yang Xiu replied, “The box plainly says, ‘one mouthful of butter cake for each person.’ How could we dare disobey the Chancellor’s command?” Though Cao Cao laughed with apparent pleasure, inwardly he detested Yang Xiu.

p.src: Cao Cao feared that someone might secretly plot against his life, and often instructed his attendants: “I am prone to killing people in my sleep; whenever I am asleep, none of you must come near me.” One day, while he was napping in his tent, his coverlet fell to the floor. One of his attendants hurried forward to cover him. Cao Cao sprang up, drew his sword, and killed the man, then returned to bed and slept; after some time he rose and feigned astonishment, asking, “Who killed my attendant?” Everyone told him the truth. Cao Cao wept bitterly and ordered that the man be buried with full honors. Everyone believed that Cao Cao truly killed people in his sleep; only Yang Xiu understood his intention. At the burial he pointed to the dead man and sighed, “It was not the Chancellor who was dreaming—it was you!” When Cao Cao heard of this, he detested Yang Xiu all the more.

p.src: Cao Cao’s third son, Cao Zhi, admired Yang Xiu’s talent and often invited him to converse through the entire night. Cao Cao discussed with his advisers the possibility of naming Cao Zhi his heir. When Cao Pi learned of this, he secretly invited Wu Zhi, magistrate of Chaoge, into his residence to confer; fearing discovery, he hid Wu Zhi inside a large hamper, claimed that it contained bolts of silk, and had it carried into the residence. Yang Xiu learned of the matter and went straight to inform Cao Cao. Cao Cao ordered men to keep watch at the gate of Cao Pi’s residence. Cao Pi hurriedly told Wu Zhi, who said, “Do not worry. Tomorrow, fill the large hamper with silk and carry it in again, thereby confounding them.” Cao Pi followed his advice and had a large hamper filled with silk carried inside. The observers searched the hamper and found that it indeed contained silk, then returned and reported to Cao Cao. Cao Cao therefore suspected Yang Xiu of slandering Cao Pi in order to harm him, and detested him all the more.

p.src: Cao Cao wished to test the abilities of Cao Pi and Cao Zhi. One day, he ordered each of them to leave through the gates of Ye, but secretly instructed the gatekeepers not to let them pass. Cao Pi arrived first. When the gatekeepers barred his way, Pi had no choice but to turn back. When Zhi learned of this, he consulted Yang Xiu. Xiu said, “You are going forth by the Prince’s command. If anyone obstructs you, simply cut him down.” Zhi agreed with his advice. When he reached the gate, the gatekeepers stopped him. Zhi rebuked them, saying, “I bear the Prince’s command! Who dares stand in my way?” He had the gatekeeper beheaded on the spot. Cao Cao therefore judged Zhi to be capable. Later, however, someone told Cao Cao, “It was Yang Xiu who taught him to do this.” Cao Cao flew into a rage and thereafter disliked Zhi as well.

p.src: Yang Xiu had also once prepared more than ten model answers for Cao Zhi, so whenever Cao Cao asked him a question, Zhi answered according to them. Whenever Cao Cao questioned Zhi about military or affairs of state, his answers came without hesitation. Cao Cao grew deeply suspicious. Later, Cao Pi secretly bribed members of Zhi’s household, stole the written answers, and brought them to Cao Cao. When Cao Cao saw them, he cried in fury, “How dare that wretch deceive me!” By then he had already resolved to kill Yang Xiu; now he merely used the charge of sowing confusion in the army as a pretext to execute him. p.src: The next day, as the army emerged at the mouth of the Xie Valley, another force came to meet it, led by the great general Wei Yan. Cao Cao called on Wei Yan to surrender, but Yan answered with bitter abuse. Cao Cao ordered Pang De to engage him. While the two generals were locked in combat, flames arose within Cao Cao’s camp. A messenger reported that Ma Chao had seized the central and rear camps. Cao Cao drew his sword and declared, “Any officer who retreats will be beheaded!” All the generals strove forward with renewed vigor. Wei Yan feigned defeat and fled. Cao Cao was just signaling his troops to turn and fight Ma Chao when he halted his horse on a high mound to watch the two armies contend. Suddenly, a body of troops burst forth before him, and a voice cried, “Wei Yan is here!” He nocked an arrow, drew his bow, and struck Cao Cao. Cao Cao tumbled from his horse. Wei Yan cast aside his bow, seized his blade, and spurred his horse up the slope to kill Cao Cao. From the side a general suddenly dashed forth, shouting, “Do not harm my lord!” It was none other than Pang De. Pang De charged forward with all his might, drove Wei Yan back, and escorted Cao Cao onward. Ma Chao had already withdrawn. Cao Cao returned to camp wounded: Wei Yan’s arrow had struck his upper lip and broken two of his front teeth, so he urgently summoned physicians to treat him. Only then did he recall Yang Xiu’s words. He had Xiu’s body recovered and buried with full honors, and at once ordered the army to return home, appointing Pang De to guard the rear. Cao Cao lay inside a felt-covered carriage, guarded on either side by his Tiger Guards as they traveled. Suddenly word came that fires had arisen on both sides of the Xie Valley hills and ambushing troops were closing in. Every man in Cao Cao’s army was stricken with fear. Indeed:
